title: LOUISVILLE VILLAGE BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Louisville Village Board met Thursday evening and made quick progress of a light agenda.

Mayor Chris Rinehart called the meeting to order, and trustees approved the meeting agenda and past meeting minutes.

The next order of business was approval of the bills.  Just as Chuck Smith started to make a motion to approve the bills, Craig Clifton said he had a question on the bills.  He noticed Clips and Tips Strays, the local group that is practicing TNR or Trap, Neuter and Return, the effort to reduce the stray cat population in Louisville.  Clifton stated he knew the board voted to make a one-time payment to the group, but it appears the group is getting more as a budget item.  This began a discussion over how items like this are paid once they are part of the annual budget and no longer required by the board.  Clifton disagreed with that interpretation.  One trustee stated they could make a motion to change make a payment to the group.  Clifton maintained that he doesn’t support the effort but, in the end, joined the other trustees in approving the bills unanimously.

At the May meeting, trustees discussed adopting a village policy that would allow the use of shipping containers as storage units within the village.  To get the ball rolling Thursday evening, the board first voted to rescind the previous Ordinance 901 which banned their use in the village.  Next, trustees hammered out the language that will be included in the new ordinance.  Among the stipulations included are adherence to village setback requirements, no unit may be placed in a front yard, they must be a solid color and include no advertising, and applications must include a site plan for how the units are placed on a village property.  There are rules for both residential and commercial use.  The mayor and the Utilities Superintendent have the discretion of what is permitted as part of the policy.  Trustees approved the agreement without dissent.  Trustees then wrestled with what to include in the application and then approved its implementation.

The board then move on to discuss whether to approve a Façade Improvement Grant Request from Josiah Adams at the art gallery and studio at 140 Chestnut.  Trustees approved the $10,025 request that is split between the village and property owner for repairs and improvements to the building in a unanimous decision.

The final action item of the meeting was the question of whether to approve a 25 cent per hour increase for the Mosquito License Compensation and the measure was approved without dissent.

During open time, several topics were raised but no vote was recorded as these items require inclusion in the meeting agenda before any action is taken.  The topics discussed included mowing on village property, positive comments about the car wash being open, the possibility of moving the oil and chipping of village streets up to mid-July was discussed but seem unlikely as vendors have their annual schedules in place months in advance and there was a discussion over where to place, “Welcome to Louisville” signs at the four entrances to Louisville.  With all business complete, the meeting adjourned.

title: CASH ELECTED STATE REPORTER
full_story:
The 2026-2027 Illinois FFA State Officer Team was elected yesterday, in Springfield.  Among those elected was Section 23 and North Clay FFA President Haven Cash, who was selected to serve as the State FFA Reporter.  Haven is the daughter of Lisa and Dustin Cash.  Katrina Van Dyke is the agriculture teacher and FFA Advisor at North Clay Community Unit School.

Haven was selected by a committee of agriculture industry friends, media and collegiate leaders, past state FFA officers and current FFA members.  The candidates completed a rigorous series of practicums, including a virtual round consisting of a writing exercise, a prepared speech, and a test on Illinois agricultural education and FFA, as well as an in-person round held at Lincoln Land Community College on Saturday, April 18th.  The in-person round included a general interview, an impromptu scenario, a facilitation exercise, and a group activity.  Haven was one of the ten candidates eligible for six Illinois FFA Major State Officer positions.  Here is a portion of Havens interview…

After an exciting morning election session, the following individuals were elected to major state office.  President: Bryer Nelson of the Canton FFA, Vice President: Collin Johnson of the Franklin FFA, Reporter: Haven Cash of the North Clay FFA, Secretary: Owen Rigg of the Williamsfield FFA, Treasurer: Lane Perry of the Marshall FFA, and Sentinel: Levi German of the Nokomis FFA Chapter.

These six student leaders will spend the next year traveling to visit chapters, facilitate workshops, and represent Illinois agricultural education.

More than 5,000 FFA members, advisors, and guests attended the 98th annual Illinois State FFA Convention.

title: FRANK & BRIGHT FLAG EXCHANGE
full_story:
Frank & Bright Funeral Home will once again host its annual Flag Exchange today from 8 am until 6 pm at the funeral home.  This is a one-day-only event.

You are invited to bring in a well-served US flag and exchange it for a new 3′ x 5′ outdoor American flag, made in the U.S.A.  One complimentary flag will be offered per household.  Additional flags may be purchased at a modest cost.

Ryan Muskopf, Daniel Fopay, Robert Bruns, and the staff of Frank & Bright Funeral Home are hosting the Flag Exchange as a way to honor current and former members of the armed forces, law enforcement, and all of our first responders.

title: 250 YEAR CELEBRATION

title: LOUISVILLE DONATES TO CATS
full_story:
The Village of Louisville, is continuing its proactive approach to address the local stray cat overpopulation, awarding a $1,500 donation to Clip and Tip Strays (C.A.T.S.), for ongoing Trap-Neuter-Release (TNR) efforts within village limits.

This funding will directly support spaying and neutering stray, feral, and community cats; an effective, humane and long-term solution to reduce overpopulation.  Through planned, coordinated efforts with neighborhood caretakers and residents, C.A.T.S. identifies targeted cat colonies, then safely traps cats, and transports them to its monthly low-cost clinic in Flora for sterilization.

The Village of Louisville has had 34 cats sterilized with last year’s allocation of $1,500 and donations from the community to an out-of-county-based TNR nonprofit.

“We want to stay ahead of the problem,” said Louisville Mayor Chris Rinehart.  “This year, we’re continuing those efforts to humanely control, and ultimately reduce, the size of stray cat colonies within Louisville.”

To date, C.A.T.S. has identified 12 stray cat colonies in Louisville.  Its board members Nicola Wattles and Belinda Rueter, residents of Louisville, have been actively working in seven colonies for several months.

Sterilized cats are less likely to wander, spray, or engage in aggressive behavior, leading to fewer complaints and a more harmonious community for both residents and animals.

Clip and Tip Strays (C.A.T.S.), a volunteer-powered nonprofit based in Flora, is dedicated to improving the lives of stray and feral cats throughout Clay County.  The organization sponsors a monthly low-cost Spay & Neuter Clinic on the second Tuesday of each month at the Wags and Wash Salon, where a licensed traveling veterinarian sterilizes up to 40 pre-registered cats in a single day.

With costs of just $60 for a male cat neuter and $80 for a female cat spay, the clinic provides an affordable option for caretakers and residents.

People can follow Clip and Tip Strays on Facebook for updates on clinic days and fundraisers or call or text 618-662-3837 for more information.

Donations can be made online at zeffy.com/en-US/organizations/clip-and-tip-strays, mailed to C.A.T.S., P.O. Box 23, Flora, or people can drop off donated items at the Country Closet in Flora towards the Clip and Tip Strays account.

Photo Caption: Louisville, IL Mayor Chris Rinehart presents the donation check to Belinda Rueter, Treasurer of Clip and Tip Strays (C.A.T.S.).

title: WILHOUR FISHING DERBY
full_story:
State Representative Blaine Wilhour will host his 4th Annual Kids Fishing Derby tomorrow, at Willow Pond, located next to the visitor center at Carlyle Lake at 801 Laker Road in Carlyle.

The event is open to children ages 4 to 15 and is being held in partnership with the Illinois Department of Natural Resources and the US Army Corps of Engineers.

The fishing derby begins at 9:00 am with presentations on water safety and instruction on how to bait a hook, cast a line, and reel in a fish.  Children must be accompanied by an adult.

“This event is a great opportunity for kids to learn how to fish for the first time or simply enjoy the outdoors at one of Illinois’ premier fishing destinations,” said Wilhour.  “We’ll once again be awarding prizes for the biggest fish caught and the most fish caught during the derby.”

For questions, please contact the district office at 618-665-4109 or online at RepWilhour.com.  The phone number at the Carlyle Lake visitor Center is 618-594-5253.

title: PLUMMER TOWN HALLS
full_story:
State Senator Jason Plummer is set to host two End of Session Town Hall events Monday, to provide residents with an update on recent legislative activity from the 2026 spring session.  The meetings will take place in Olney and in Salem.

The events are free and open to the public.  Residents are encouraged to attend to learn more about actions taken during the spring session, ask questions, and share feedback on issues important to their communities.

In Olney the meeting will be held from 5 to 6 pm at the Olney Public Library.  In Salem the meeting will be held from 7 to 8 pm at the Salem Education Center.  Residents are encouraged to attend, learn more about the spring legislative session, and ask questions about state government.

title: S.U.R.E. SYMPOSIUM
full_story:
The Clay County Health Department is collaborating with the Coalition Against Drug Abuse of Clay County, the Clay County Board, SIU School of Medicine, and Birth to Five Illinois to bring the second Substance Use Resource & Education Symposium or S.U.R.E Symposium to Clay County on August 11th.  Registration will begin at 8:30 am at the Oil Belt Christian Service Camp.

The goal of the S.U.R.E. Symposium is to bring together local agencies, experts, and community members to provide a safe space to learn about substance abuse prevention, recovery, and what happens after.

Lunch will be provided to the first 200 who register, and continuing education units are pending.  Register by going to tinyurl.com/SURE2026 or use the QR code on the health department’s website.  This years symposium registration is being covered by the Clay County Board Opioid Settlement.

title: TICK SPECIES SPREADING
full_story:
Social media is abuzz with news about ticks and tick-borne diseases actively spreading across Illinois, with many counties confirming several species.

Some of the increased talk comes from more awareness of ticks and their dangers, Jenny Buttaccio, Illinois Lyme Association (ILA) communications director, told FarmWeek.

However, Illinois has ticks converging from the north and south.  Different tick species at different life stages are peaking at different times.  “So, it is very alarming,” said Samantha Kerr, the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH)’s vector surveillance and control program manager.

Many Illinois counties have lone star ticks, blacklegged ticks and dog ticks.  Several counties have all three, according to the IDPH tick surveillance maps.

“The geographic range of different species is expanding,” said Chris Stone, University of Illinois medical entomologist, who noted the Gulf Coast tick is also present in southern and parts of central Illinois.

The blacklegged tick, associated with Lyme disease, was more concentrated in northern Illinois, but is trickling south to central Illinois.  At the same time, the lone star tick that can cause Alpha-gal syndrome, an allergic reaction to red meat, is moving from the south toward central Illinois.  Illinois is already in the top 13 states of Alpha-gal cases in the nation, Buttaccio said.

Part of the uptick of ticks in Illinois is due to warmer winters and longer, warmer seasons.  The invasive Asian longhorned tick, which attacks large livestock rather than people, is also a threat in Illinois.  Information about ticks and their diseases in Illinois is available on the Illinois Tickborne Disease Dashboard website experience.arcgis.com.

Last month, US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. announced major initiatives to strengthen the nation’s response to Lyme disease and other tick-borne illnesses, including a multi-million-dollar pilot program focused on tick control and funding for researchers to combat Alpha-gal syndrome.

Kerr said the general advice of avoiding tick habitats is harder for farmers to follow when they are mowing grass, repairing fences and doing other outdoor work.  She recommends the use of Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellents, wearing permethrin-treated clothing, using a lint roller to remove possible ticks, doing a thorough tick check and showering within a couple of hours of potential exposure.

You can have a big impact on protecting yourself by doing small things, Stone said.  Wear long pants and clothing treated with permethrin, “It’s cheap and easy to do.”
